HEADLINE: Turnbull's tradies to be big winners from the budget
INTRO: Small and medium business will be biggest winners in Tuesday's federal budget, the main drivers of growth in Australia's economy and will therefore be the , Treasurer Scott Morrison says.
TEXT:
Small and medium business will be biggest winners in Tuesday's federal budget, the main drivers of growth in Australia's economy and will therefore be the , Treasurer Scott Morrison says.

Mr Morrison told AFR Weekend that the little spare revenue the government had to spend would be largely dedicated to SMEs because, as the economy transitioned away from mining, SMEs were "the hope of the side".

His comments all but confirm earlier speculation that the budget will contain measures similar to last year's $20,000 instant asset write-off for small business. That scheme could be expanded and extended beyond its expiry date of June 30, 2017, or be augmented by other similar measures.

"They're the hope of the side, they work hard, earn more, the budget has to back them, that's the bottom line," the Treasurer said.

The budget will keep alive contentious plans to deregulate university fees but the final policy will be subject to further consideration. However, it is expected that students could pay more for degrees. At present they pay 40 per cent for the cost of a degree and the government pays 60 per cent. There is speculation that ratio could be increased to 50:50.

Mr Morrison, who holds an honours degree in applied economic geography, called SMEs the "thalweg", the geographical term for the deep course of a river or stream.

He also indicated that the economic growth outlook that he significantly downgraded in December's budget update would remain relatively subdued. In his last budget in 2015, Joe Hockey included growth projections of 3.5 per cent for 2017-18 and 2018-19.

In December, Mr Morrison downgraded these to 3 per cent for each year and lowered the expectation for 2016-17 from 3.25 per cent to 2.75 per cent.

"I took a very conscious decision to try and end this process by where they have 3.5 per cent growth projections," he said.

"I just said 'no, I don't believe it'."

He said there would be "some movement" in the growth forecasts since December but they would be slight. Nor should anybody expect "wild variations" in revenue predictions since December, indicating a long road back to surplus. He rejected suggestions by some that he should simply hike the overall tax burden to hasten the return to surplus, saying the "conditions are too sensitive" and that would damage the economy.

While the bulk of tax cuts in the budget will be directed towards business in a bid to stimulate growth, including the possibility of a small company tax cut, the budget is expected to contain a small income tax cut in the form of an increase to the $80,001 income threshold at which the income tax rate rises from 32.5 per cent to 37 per cent.

Superannuation tax concessions for high income earners will also be trimmed with the proceeds to be churned back into the super savings of those on lower incomes.

There was speculation on Friday Mr Morrison would slash the $180,000 after-tax contributions limit, while the government is also set to match Labor by charging 30 per cent tax on super contributions by people who earn more than $250,000, down from the current threshold of $300,000.

Low-income and part-time workers, such as young mothers who take time off work to rear children, are expected to be given leeway to top up their super savings when they return to work.

Mr Morrison cautioned it would not be a typical budget full of measures. he said the main aim was to inspire confidence in the public that the government had a plan to grow the economy because that was the only meaningful way there would be a return to surplus.

Mr Morrison said most of the measures would be public by budget day so he could dedicate his speech to Parliament to the big picture.

"On Tuesday night, I want to talk about the economy and the plan because that's what people want to hear and see. To give them the confidence they need to go out and keep doing what they are doing. I don't want them to be knocked off course."

He said while there may have been a revenue boost from an unexpected lift in the iron ore prices, there was a multitude of factors that countered that.

"We have seen lots of movements in different indicators whether it's been stock market, oil price, the Tapis, iron ore prices, the world GDP forecasts from the IMF. There's been a lot of moving parts over the last several months, in particular. You will see next Tuesday how they have all reconciled when it comes to what Treasury has put forward in their view about the Australian economy. "

HEADLINE: Chefs search for cuisine-fusing zen
INTRO: Mash-ups the dish of the day at top eateries.
TEXT:
Mash-ups the dish of the day at top eateries.

Fusion food should not be confusing, one of Australia's leading chefs says.

Some top restaurants are mixing traditional French and Italian cuisine with Japanese ingredients and techniques.

LuMi Bar and Dining chef Federico Zanellato said creating traditional Italian food with Japanese ingredients was "very risky" and at times was "difficult to match". He said it was important for chefs to find the right balance. Some of his dishes looked Japanese but tasted Italian.

"My background is Italian. I was born there but I've spent most of my time travelling and working elsewhere, including in Japan," he said. "The menu at LuMi is a mix of my experience. We didn't plan on it having an Italian and Japanese fusion, it just happened and it's evolved."

LuMi, in Pyrmont in Sydney, has been listed in 2016's The Australian Financial Review Top Restaurants, presented by Qantas.

On Monday night, the nation's top chefs and restaurateurs will battle it out in the only national restaurant awards program of its kind to be decided by their peers.

Awards co-director Jill Dupleix said Tetsuya Wakuda started the fusion trend 27 years ago, when he learned French techniques from Tony Bilson and combined them with his obsession for the ingredients and flavours of Japan at his first restaurant, Ultimo's.

"By the time he opened Tetsuya's, then in Rozelle, he was really creating a new Japanese-French cuisine," Ms Dupleix said.

"We called it fusion then. Now it's just called a mash-up. It's a very natural progression for young Australian chefs of different heritages to combine their own cooking style with Japanese influences.

Michael Ryan, the chef and owner of Provenance, a restaurant in north-east Victoria, said studying Japanese at university and an interest in the culture led him to include Japanese flavours and techniques in his cooking.

"I do what I like to cook," he said. "There's nothing worse than a menu that is made up to look like a theme park. I want my guests to try the food, to have it evoke or make them think of their trip to Japan."

Awards co-director Terry Durack said it was all about umami, the savouriness that is known as the "fifth taste".

"Fermented foods such as miso and soy add greater depth and definition, or a nuance that wasn't there before," he said.

"Australian chefs are using it to add another dimension to their cuisine."

Ms Dupleix said fusing cultures was not about some hideous "Frankenfood" hybrid cuisine that should never be forced together.

"Japanese cuisine has so many shadows and lights that in the right hands it insinuates itself very naturally and sympathetically into a different cuisine," she said.

The Top 100 list and the winners will be announced at a gala awards ceremony in Sydney on Monday.

For more information and to view the full list of 500 restaurants visit www.australiastoprestaurants.com.

HEADLINE: Morrison cops more flak over Kidman
INTRO: Treasurer Scott Morrison was accused of playing politics with foreign investment after he decided to stop a Chinese-led consortium buying Australia's biggest private landholder, buying S.Kidman and Co.
TEXT:
Treasurer Scott Morrison was accused of playing politics with foreign investment after he decided to stop a Chinese-led consortium buying Australia's biggest private landholder, buying S.Kidman and Co.

National Farmers Federation Vice President Fiona Simson said the veto over 1.3 per cent of Australia's land mass would confuse and send mixed signals to foreign investors, which he said was badly needed in the agriculture industry. Future Farmers Network board director Sam Trethewey questioned if the decision was xenophobic.

Mr Morrison, who had previously given himself until after the election to decide, announced on Friday a 'preliminary decision' that the sale was against the national interest.

The deal did not give local bidders enough of an opportunity, the land size was too large and he needed to consider maintaining support within the electorate for foreign investment, Mr Morrison said.

Nationals Leader Barnaby Joyce said the decision "shows our nation has the capacity to say yes - and often does - to foreign investment, but is also prepared to say no".

While officials from China's Ministry of Commerce said they hoped Australia would reconsider, rival domestic bidders for the company were moving in.

Labor Shadow Minister for Trade and Investment Penny Wong said Mr Morrison had made the decision a "political plaything".

Australian Rural Capital and China-based Dakang Australia Holdings last week pipped Australian bidders with a $370.7 million offer for S.Kidman and Co. This is the second time a deal to buy the company has hit a roadblock due to national security concerns. The latest agreement no longer includes Anna Creek near the weapons testing site at Woomera in South Australia, which Mr Morrison said last time was the reason he blocked the sale.

"Is this is about appeasing the xenophobic dark side of many Australians and clinging to polls?" Mr Trethewey tweeted.

The company, which covers almost 11 million hectares of cattle stations - including the world's largest, Anna Creek - was offered for sale this time last year through EY.

Dakang Australia is 51 per cent owned by Dakang Pasture Farming and 49 per cent owned by Shanghai CRED Real Estate Stock Co. Dakang was set to acquire 80 per cent of S.Kidman & Co and Australian Rural Capital was to acquire 20 per cent of the company.

Trucking magnate Lindsay Fox, who also wanted to buy the S.Kidman & Co property portfolio, supported the decision. "I guess the Treasurer has to do what he has to do," Mr Fox he said.

Other bidders also expressed support for Mr Morrison. DomaCom chief executive Arthur Naoumidis, who attempted to buy the land, said it was "very pleasing" that the government had heeded the outpouring of public sentiment.

"What the DomaCom campaign clearly demonstrated that there is genuine public interest in keeping the iconic Kidman pastoral station in Australian hands, and that 'mum and dad' investors want to have a stake in this country's agricultural heritage."

The general manager of Shanghai CRED Real Estate Stock, Gui Guojie, pledged to sponsor Port Adelaide Football Club to the tune of millions of dollars before the deal was inked.

Some Chinese media reports had emphasised how incredible it was that a company was able to purchase such as sizeable amount of a country, an area equivalent to Zhejiang province in South China.

Key points

Treasurer accused of playing politics by giving Chinese-led consortium thumbs-down.

Signals 'confusing'.

HEADLINE: 'Value capture' plan splits developers
INTRO: Prime Minister Malcolm Turnbull's plan to fund infrastructure through the use of so-called value capture has exposed divisions within the development industry.
TEXT:
Prime Minister Malcolm Turnbull's plan to fund infrastructure through the use of so-called value capture has exposed divisions within the development industry.

Announcing a plan to use cheaper Commonwealth borrowing for approved projects on Friday, Mr Turnbull said developments needed to harness the boost in property values that resulted from them.

"We need a cultural gear change in the way that we look at urban infrastructure," Mr Turnbull said. "Transport infrastructure changes a community. It can change it for good or ill. It can unite a community or it can divide it. It can create enormous value, enormous value in real estate, enormous value in added amenity. It has to be looked at in a complete urban context."

But the announcements by the Prime Minister at the Smart Cities Plan summit in Melbourne, did not excite some developers.

The Property Council of Australia welcomed the overall plan but criticised a notion it called "vague and without definition".

"Value capture is not a magic pudding and the risks of damaging the economy with naive approaches are very real," council chief executive Ken Morrison said.

"Does the federal Government propose introducing new taxes, or just encourage state governments to do so? At the moment we have no idea."

Lara Poloni, the Australia-New Zealand chief executive of consulting firm AECOM, who presented in one of the closed sessions at the summit, was more positive about the notion.

"Today there was broad acknowledgement that value capture is one of a suite of options that is available to fast track city-shaping infrastructure," Ms Poloni told AFR Weekend. "It is clear that some people support the concept whereas others are concerned that it is just another tax."

It was a practice widely accepted and used elsewhere, Ms Poloni said.

"Value capture recognises that some direct beneficiaries do not always contribute their fair share and receive an unintended windfall.

International projects like London's CrossRail are capturing an equitable share of these indirect benefits to help fund the project, which go well beyond the direct beneficiaries within a precinct."

The federal government is already looking closely at the how value capture could work in practice, through a parliamentary inquiry into how transport infrastructure stimulates development and economic activity. In testimony to the inquiry earlier this month, senior executives at developer Centurion Group, which represents China Rail, explained how a new rail service from Wollongong to Campbelltown would make possible a massive housing plan in the area.

The so-called Macarthur plan envisages 100,000 to 150,000 new homes in the area opened up by the new rail.

"It is from the generation of those new homes, from our enabling transport, that the plan is to have a value-creation levy-charge, contribution—from those new homes," chief executive Dr Patrick Yu told the inquiry.

On Centurion's estimate $250 per square metre could be levied, on new houses conservatively estimated to be 150 square metres. That would raise $3.75 billion.

The tax should not be imposed until the infrastructure was under way, the inquiry was told, with Mr Yu adding that China rail had the backing of local industry funds and China Development Bank.

Other groups were cautious on Friday.

"The [newly created] infrastructure financing unit should examine how best to tap these sources of funding for different projects," Ai Group chief executive Innes Willox said.

"In whatever way they are financed, these investments need to be rigorously and independently assessed for their impact on Australian living standards and not captured for near-term political advantage."

Fund manager Charter Hall said Australia was well placed to fund infrastructure investments.

"We look forward to the early involvement of industry who can add value through innovation and investment, which will provide the community with better and more certain outcomes," group chief executive David Harrison said.

HEADLINE: We're all tax avoiders. Get over it
INTRO: If they're legal it's not evasion, it's only avoidance.
TEXT:
If they're legal it's not evasion, it's only avoidance.

With only two weeks until the Tax Office's final deadline to lodge our 2014-15 tax returns, Prime Minister Malcolm Turnbull gave taxpayers a handy piece of tax advice.

"Tax avoidance is legal," he told Radio 3AW.

"It may be undesirable and you may want to change the law to prevent it, [but] tax evasion is what is illegal."

Predictably Twitterverse went straight to peak outrage. Excitable younger politicians like Liberal MP Alex Hawke and Labor's Sam Dastyari traded blows over which side most channelled Gordon Gekko.

Labor immediately dug up an old quote from Assistant Treasurer Kelly O'Dwyer saying "that tax avoidance, structuring your affairs to avoid paying tax, is in fact against the law".

Everyone knows you shouldn't tax advice from your mates at the pub. But what about tax advice from your Prime Minister?

Desk-bound wage slaves quietly called their accountants to check whether it could possibly be true.

"Oh, yes. We're all tax avoiders," said a cheery local accountant. Let's call him, "John".

"Tax avoidance is not nice but no one is going to give you a prize if you are over-paying tax, and you don't claim the legal deductions entitled to you."

In the words of the late Kerry Packer: "Of course I am minimising my tax and if anybody in this country doesn't minimise their tax they want their heads read because as a government, I can tell you you're not spending it that well that we should be donating extra."

So - just asking for a friend - how does one become a successful and legal tax avoider? And what's the difference between a legal - albeit undesirable - tax avoider and a potential jailbird tax evader?

"You can just do vanilla things like claiming your laptop as a work deduction, claiming steel-capped boots, negatively gear your property for wealth creation or minimise your tax through superannuation to save for your retirement in the best way available to you," said John the Accountant.

The murky area of legal tax minimisation has become a hot political issue because Labor wants to limit negative gearing to new properties from 2017 to eliminate what it sees as excesses in the system in which the wealthy negatively gear multiple properties for big tax benefits.

Shadow treasurer Chris Bowen helpfully pointed to Mr Turnbull's comments from 2005 in which he said negative gearing - currently used by about one and half million Australians - was a form of tax avoidance and one of the few legal ways for average wage earners to reduce their tax.

While Australia has some of the toughest anti-avoidance measures in the world through Part IVA - the general anti-avoidance rule for income tax - the big test for the Tax Commissioner is whether the main purpose of a transaction is to avoid tax, rather than say, wealth creation.

The tax evaders are the people cooking their books or operating in the cash economy.

So who is the biggest tax crook? A property developer with dozens of negatively geared property and zero taxable income, or the local babysitter paid cash in hand?

"Definitely the babysitter," said John the Accountant.

"Unless she earns below the low-income tax threshold and can prove babysitting is a hobby".

HEADLINE: APLNG boost for Origin sales despite soft prices
INTRO: A strong start up of the $25 billion Australian Pacific LNG project in Queensland has driven a surge in Origin Energy's quarterly oil and gas sales, more than offsetting the impact of soft prices.
TEXT:
A strong start up of the $25 billion Australian Pacific LNG project in Queensland has driven a surge in Origin Energy's quarterly oil and gas sales, more than offsetting the impact of soft prices.

However, the business is still expected to show a net loss for the full year.

Eleven LNG cargoes were shipped from the project in the three months ended March 31, helping lift oil and gas revenue 45 per cent to $316.4 million from the year-earlier period. Production jumped 65 per cent to the equivalent of 60.9 petajoules.

Most of the cargoes shipped from the Gladstone project went to APLNG's biggest customer, Sinopec, said David Baldwin, Origin's head of integrated gas. Another four cargoes have been exported this month, and the second train at the site is on track to start up in the December half, he said.

But pricing achieved under the deliveries was on the soft side, with JPMorgan's Mark Busuttil noting that Origin's LNG prices were the lowest realised by any of the Australian producers. The average price was $US6.17 per million British thermal units, compared to $US6.24 for Santos's GLNG venture, $US6.84 for Oil Search's Papua New Guinea venture and $US9.39 for Woodside Petroleum's Pluto LNG, he said.

The strengthening in the Australian dollar through the quarter also affected Origin's oil and gas sales prices across the board in the quarter.

The better-than-expected early performance from APLNG confirmed recent comments from the LNG head at Bechtel, the US engineering company that built all three Curtis Island LNG plants.

"Pleasingly, daily production rates from Australia Pacific LNG's first production train have exceeded design nameplate capacity of 4.5 million tonnes per annum," Mr Baldwin said.

Origin's foundation partner in APLNG, ConocoPhillips, said overnight that the second production train at the 9 million-tonnes-a-year APLNG venture was expected to start production in the December quarter. The first shipment left Gladstone port on January 9, slightly later than targeted.

Origin said it now expected revenues from the first train to flow through into its results starting on March 1. As a result it has increased its guidance for the LNG division's underlying earnings before interest, tax, depreciation and amortisation for the 2015-16 financial year to $100 million-$150 million, up from its February guidance of $30 million-$80 million.

But guidance for the LNG businesses's contribution to underlying net profit remains a loss of $170 million-$220 million after funding and other costs. Forecasts for profits from APLNG and Australia's other new LNG projects have been slashed since oil prices started their dramatic decline in mid-2014.

Still, year-to-date revenues from Origin's oil and gas business are now running 6 per cent above a year earlier, at $735.1 million, after lagging behind at the first half stage.

HEADLINE: 'Signs of life' finally emerge as term deposit rates rise
INTRO: Banks have nudged up interest rates on term deposits this year, a sign the very skinny returns from bank deposits may be starting to lift from historic lows.
TEXT:
Banks have nudged up interest rates on term deposits this year, a sign the very skinny returns from bank deposits may be starting to lift from historic lows.

Average interest rates on a range of term deposits have risen since the beginning of this year, especially among three-month, six-month and nine-month products, figures from interest rate comparison website Mozo show. While the increases are small, at about 10 basis points, Mozo says there is an industry-wide trend towards deposit rates increasing for the first time since 2011.

Senior bankers have also highlighted the trend, which if sustained, may limit the boost that banks' profit margins receive from the round of home loan interest rate rises last year.

Kirsty Lamont from Mozo said that since January there had been 87 interest rate increases in term deposit products, compared with 17 decreases, and the rises were the first "signs of life" in that market for several years.

"It shows that the banks are becoming more interested in deposit funding for the first time really since 2011," Ms Lamont said.

The increases, however, are not dramatic. The average rate on a three-month deposit has risen 11 basis points to 2.58 per cent since January, six-month rates are up 9 basis point to 2.69 per cent and nine-month rates have increased by the same amount, to 2.52 per cent. Ms Lamont said these rates were still lower than what is available through a "bonus" at-call savings account, which require customers to meet conditions such as making a minimum deposit each month.

"Although term deposits are showing signs of life and we are seeing increases, they are still a long way off being competitive," Ms Lamont said.

Even so, the trend has caught the eye of senior bankers, as increased competition for deposits tends to raise funding costs, which have been pushed higher on wholesale debt markets this year.

Deposit pricing became a key issue in years after the global financial crisis, as banks blamed a "war for deposits" for unpopular moves to increase their mortgage interest rates. While few are predicting such fierce competition for deposits this time around, recent rises may also reflect banks' responding to rising wholesale funding costs, which have risen this year.

The Reserve Bank's Financial Stability Review, published this month, said the higher cost of wholesale funding was not yet affecting rates on term deposits, but "competition for deposits may increase if conditions in wholesale funding markets become less accommodative in the period ahead".

HEADLINE: Surfstitch lost after CEO wipe-out
INTRO: Australia's surfwear companies have a history of extraordinary growth followed by sudden wipe-outs so it is no surprise investors are nervous about the information vacuum surrounding Surfstitch.
TEXT:
Australia's surfwear companies have a history of extraordinary growth followed by sudden wipe-outs so it is no surprise investors are nervous about the information vacuum surrounding Surfstitch.

There has been radio silence from the online action sports retailer since its co-founder and chief executive Justin Cameron quit abruptly six weeks ago with news he was considering a possible takeover bid.

The extraordinary turn of events has understandably rattled investors. One substantial investor describes it as "funky, a bit strange and weird". Things came to a head this week when the company's stock sank back towards its $1 issue price on the assumption that no news was bad news.

Chairman Howard McDonald's phone has been ringing off the hook with shareholders wanting to know what is going on. Some have been asking him to at least make a statement to the market to give some assurances about the company's performance.

McDonald is the kind of chairman who likes to have all the information in front of him and something to say before going to the market. The sudden departure of Cameron, who resigned in a one-line email, destabilised the company at a time when it needed to restructure and consolidate following a string of acquisitions.

The company's position will become clearer next week when McDonald is expected to update the market on its current position. Cameron's intentions remain a mystery though and there has been no contact between him, the rumoured private equity bidder and the board since the resignation bombshell.

People close to Cameron believe a takeover is still in the works though. They say Cameron, who started the company from his Sydney garage and is said to be frustrated with the market's reaction to a profit downgrade earlier this year, is a savvy entrepreneur who would not have resigned if he did not think there was a realistic chance of taking the company private.

There are also suggestions UK fast fashion outfit ASOS and Chinese e-commerce giant Alibaba also have looked at the company

Others say the chance of a bid is 50:50 or less and even then would a private equity firm be prepared to pay $2 per share or more, which is what it raised equity at last year, for a company that is currently valued at a little above $1.

Responding to criticism he had left the market uninformed, McDonald told Chanticleer he takes umbrage with suggestions he has put up the drawbridge. He has had 30 briefings with shareholders this week, with four on Friday afternoon alone.

He will be working his two co-chief executives Justin Stone is in London and Lex Penderson in California, who have been reviewing the European and US operations, over the weekend to reaffirm where the company is at and there are expectations the market will be updated next week.

McDonald also wants to strengthen management where the departure of Cameron, who ran the company from a high level, left gaps.

He is expected to appoint a new Australian-based chief operating officer (COO) who will act as a bridge between the two co-chiefs in London and California.

The message to shareholders is that strategy is on track but the business needs to go through a period of consolidating its brands and e-commerce platforms after a period of rapid growth as the company focused on beefing up its content assets.

Not everyone is happy with the company's approach which is reflected in the sagging price. Mark Maloney, the executive chairman of private equity firm Intrepic, picked up just under 5 per cent of the company when Cameron acquired his Garage Entertainment business last year.

Maloney, who ran his family's mining services company MAC Services which was sold for $650 million in 2010, is seeking a directorship at Surfstitch and is believed to have an eye on the chairman's role.

Kidman deal on hold

The upcoming federal election has effectively killed off the Chinese takeover of S.Kidman & Co.

The political environment makes it impossible for Treasurer Scott Morrison to approve the sale of the country's largest landholder to foreign interests.

The sensible thing for China-based Dakang Holdings and Kidman to take the offer for around 11 million hectares of cattle stations off the table and sit tight until things calm down.

Dakang has until May 3 to respond but it is safe to assume it will withdraw rather than trying to tweak an offer which will pass this "national interest" test this side of an election, or even shortly after.

Initially Kidman & Co hoped the Treasurer would put off making a decision until after the election to avoid any political backlash from the Nationals but sign off on it then.

PNG ruling blows defence

Papua New Guinea's Supreme Court blew Broadspectrum's last line of defence against Ferrovial's $813 million takeover bid out of the water this week when it ruled the Manus Island detention centre was illegal.

Ferrovial says its $1.50 per share offer had always factored in the risks associated with the detention centre contracts and it is happy with the outcome.

That is true to a point but there is no denying in an ideal world it would have secured the bid and kept the revenues from Manus Island to restructure the maintenance and services businesses which attracted it to Broadspectrum in the first place.
